extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of education, pedagogy, and social anthropology; educators interested in theory of motives and ceremonial behaviour
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts theoretical criteria for using motives (senses, organic feelings, emotions) in education and analytic criteria for interpreting ceremonial forms of address and linguistic etiquette in societies. Covers practical guidance on punishments/rewards and how language/ritual signals social structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senses as primary motives
rubrics_metrics.description: The pleasures, the pains, and the privations of the senses are the earliest and the most unfailing, if not also the strongest, of motives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sensory pleasures and pains (e.g., tactile, gustatory, auditory, visual pleasures) as primary tools of influence in education and discipline because they are early-developing and reliably effective. Examples: employing pleasant sensory experiences as rewards; noting that sensory pleasures can be counted on with considerable certainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include organic sensibility beyond the five senses
rubrics_metrics.description: The omission of the varied organic susceptibility leaves a wide gap; pleasures and pains arising from digestion, circulation, respiration, muscular and nervous integrity are among our very strongest motives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize and use organic sensations (hunger, fatigue, bodily comfort/discomfort, nervous well-being) as motives separate from the five classic senses. Examples: appetite and nourishment as incentives; muscular activity as source of pleasure and pain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Muscular activity and exercise as motivational resources
rubrics_metrics.description: The muscular system is the seat of a mass of sensibility, pleasurable and painful: the pleasures of healthy exercise, the pains of privation of exercise, and the pains of extreme fatigue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide full scope for healthy physical activity as a reward and avoid forcing exercise beyond capacity. In discipline, milder penalties for the young may be irksomeness of restraint; for adults, fatigue is used as a severe punishment. Balance exercise to harness its motivational value without causing harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid monotony, confinement, and nervous over-exertion
rubrics_metrics.description: The state denominated 'tedium' is nervous uneasiness caused by undue exercise of any portion of the nervous system; acute sufferings of the nervous system arise from confinement, monotony, and certain penal impositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design tasks and punishments to avoid prolonged monotony or confinement which produce deep nervous suffering. Be cautious about using monotonous or nerve-targeting punishments; consider ethical and developmental effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use nourishment as a calibrated motive, not severe deprivation
rubrics_metrics.description: Starvation, deficiency and inferiority of food are connected with depression and misery; punishing by loss of a meal is a telling motive, but absolutely diminishing available nutriment is severe; habitual regimen should be neither too low nor too high to permit variations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Food can be an effective incentive or mild punishment (e.g., withholding a meal) but must never approach actual deprivation. Maintain baseline adequate regimen so increases or reductions in food serve as meaningful but ethical motivators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical punishments are powerful but must be strictly limited
rubrics_metrics.description: Inflictions of caning and flogging operate upon the organ of the sense of touch but are pains of organic life; like all physical acute pains they are powerful deterring influences; the limitations to their use demand a rigorous handling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge the deterrent power of corporal punishment while imposing rigorous ethical, legal, and proportional constraints. Consider alternatives and be mindful of long-term harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer sensory pleasures as incentives; avoid sensory punishments
rubrics_metrics.description: The ordinary five senses contain many considerable sensibilities to pleasure and pain. The pleasures can be largely made use of as incentives. We do not punish by bad odors, nor by bitter tastes; harsh and grating sounds may be torturing but are not used in discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit positive sensory experiences for reinforcement rather than employing aversive sensory punishments, which are uncommon and often barbarous. Use pleasant sensory modalities (taste, touch, sound, sight) to reward learning and good conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish privation from transient craving (hunger)
rubrics_metrics.description: Privation is the positive deficiency of nourishing material in the blood; hunger is the craving of the stomach at its usual times. There may be plenty of material though one suffers stomachic hunger. Punishing by the loss of a single meal is unimportant to general vigor yet effective as a motive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using food-related motives, understand physiological distinctions: temporary hunger (withheld meal) can be an effective, low-severity motivator; true privation (malnutrition) is unacceptable and severe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Higher emotions complicate simple sensory motives
rubrics_metrics.description: Few of the simple sensational effects are obtained in purity, that is, without the intermingling of emotions. The higher emotions are a perplexing department of motives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accounting for emotions is essential: emotional states interact with sensory motives. Educational design should consider pride, shame, sympathy, affection, etc., not only raw sensory rewards/pains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret terms of address as indicators of social relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Words such as 'servant' or 'thy servant' in historical texts signify subjection and the state of a captive; 'thy son' used to a ruler is originally equivalent to 'thy servant.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In analysis of ceremonial speech, treat self-abasing or filial terms as evidence of subordination and historical relations of power. Use literal/formal phrasing in texts as cues to social status and political structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complimentary and eulogistic speech reflect and spread social hierarchy
rubrics_metrics.description: Eulogistic phrases, first used to supreme men, descend to men of less authority and become generalized complimentary forms of speech; extreme hyperbole in eulogy indicates high development of militant/deified rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the presence, intensity, and diffusion of flattering epithets (e.g., 'Son of Heaven', 'Master of Life') as a metric for the degree to which society is organized around a deified or militaristic ruler. Track how such forms spread to infer social diffusion of hierarchy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linguistic devices that maintain distance (avoidance of names/pronouns)
rubrics_metrics.description: Special vocabulary, avoidance of proper names, and avoidance or perversion of personal pronouns are used to exalt superiors and abase inferiors; e.g., reverential forms, substitution of periphrases for a ruler's name, distinct pronouns by class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess levels of ceremonial distance by examining (a) whether proper names are avoided, (b) existence of special honorific vocabulary, and (c) pronominal distinctions or avoidance. Examples from Siam, Japan, China, Samoa, Mexico illustrate these phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of ceremonial speech correlates with social organization
rubrics_metrics.description: Where there is no subordination, speeches which exalt the person spoken to and abase the person speaking do not arise; conversely, in societies with absolute personal government, verbal self-humiliations and verbal exaltations assume exaggerated forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the presence/absence and extent of ceremonial address forms (humility of speaker, exaltation of addressee) as indicators of the social/political organization—militant/despotic vs. industrial/free societies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using extreme sensory punishments historically associated with barbarity
rubrics_metrics.description: The pains of sight reach the highest acuteness, but as punishment they are found only in the most barbarous codes; harsh sensory punishments (bad odors, bitter tastes) are generally unused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refrain from employing extreme or exotic sensory punishments; consider historical examples as anti-patterns. Focus on constructive and ethically acceptable motivators and sanctions.
